cards.title: The agent-payments wedge
cards.text: A stablecoin send has no chargeback, and stablecoin issuers freeze on legal process, not on a customer's complaint. Spend rules record what the agent was allowed to do. Nothing records what it expected or whether that came true. That second half is the wedge.

sections.title: Bull vs Bear
sections.tagline: Activity over size, applied to agent payments: counts say yes, filtered volume says not yet.

blocks.text: Crypto theses pick a side. I name which signal each side rests on, and what would settle it.

rows.text: [x402 reported](https://www.rzlt.io/blog/agentic-payments-2026-x402-explainer) over 165M agent transactions by April, about half of them tests. As of April 2026; re-read due.

The [median L2 fee](https://www.growthepie.com/answers/are-ethereum-l2-fees-getting-cheaper) fell from 20¢ in February 2024 to 0.06¢ in April 2026, cheap enough for machine-sized payments. Ramps are not in this number; an agent's float has to get on-chain first.

rows.signal: Volume with tests and wash trades removed
rows.text: [Allium, via Nevermined](https://nevermined.ai/blog/stablecoin-payments-ai-agents-statistics): about $1.6M a month of agent volume on the strictest filter. Re-read due.

The [OCC stablecoin rule](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2026/nr-occ-2026-92.html) takes effect 2027-01-18. A [procedural vote](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/crypto-market-structure-bill-fails-in-senate-vote-49-50) on the market-structure bill failed 49 to 50 on 2026-09-15.

My read: the liability rule gets written where the loss lands. On cards that is Visa and Mastercard's rulebook, pushed by the card issuers who eat the fraud. On-chain there is no rulebook yet. The call below counts only the card side, because I can check it.

rows.signal: Who pays when an agent exceeds its mandate
rows.text: [Footnote 25 of Kyle's stablecoin post](https://kylelibra.substack.com/p/a-lot-of-what-people-think-about): crypto payments will have to address chargebacks and fraud liability "to some extent to be viable." For agents, I think that starts with a record of what the user told the agent. Today it is [unsettled](https://worldpay.com/en/insights/articles/agentic-commerce-liability-is-still-being-written), and the first network rule that requires an intent record decides it.

Volume is the lagging bet. The liability rule is the leading one. My read: 1 in 3 that Visa, Mastercard or a top-10 US card issuer has a rule in effect by 2027-06-30 requiring a record of what the user told the agent. Announcements without an effective date do not count. I will post the outcome either way.
No network rule is in effect by mid-2027, and I have spent about three weeks. ARCS records human decisions this way today; it does not yet do signed agent mandates.

rows.signal: The odds moved with the wording
rows.text: My own estimate swung from about 1 in 4 to about 3 in 5 depending on how the rule was worded, so I wrote the resolution rule above before picking a number. The inputs were my judgment, not data; the simulation is on request. The base rate of a network rule drives most of what spread is left; I re-mark at each Visa and Mastercard rules release.

rows.signal: I build the thing that would benefit
rows.text: So I am not the one who should grade it. Gravity resolves it, and the If I'm wrong row says what ARCS does not do yet.

groups.label: How I could read it wrong

rows.text: Tests and self-dealing loops inflate the count, so I discount it by the half that is tests.

Visa and Mastercard run agent payments on tokenized cards ([PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/credit-cards/2026/cards-make-their-case-in-an-agentic-world/)). None of it shows on-chain, so on-chain volume undercounts agent demand.
An operator's agents paying its own services look like wash trades, so the strict filter may drop real use. I have not tested this.
If spend-rule vendors start logging what the agent expected next to what happened, the gap closes without me.
[Day 0 to day 210](https://status.arcs.care): 6,195 commits by Nov 5, built solo and run in production. Every number is read from the repository.
Answers RFP questions and cites the clause, or says the document is silent. [Four short videos](https://good.arcs.care/rfp-engine) and [its source](https://github.com/flashesofbrilliance/rfp-engine).

[The tool these records come from](https://app.arcs.care): you ask a question; it writes a dated record. [11 saved decisions from outside users, 0 outcomes closed](https://status.arcs.care); 5 people behind them, from a production read on request. Nobody outside has logged an outcome yet.

[48 beliefs overturned since June](https://status.arcs.care/beliefs), about 10 a month, dated on a public timeline; the belief and test behind each are on request. For example, "a green production build means the database works", killed 2026-06-03 by the first real query against prod. 20 changed the rulebook.
[32 claims about my work](https://zach.md/proof), each linked to its record: 23 public, 8 on request, and the 1 I cannot show yet, named.
[35 field notes](https://good.arcs.care/blog/nftt), each written from a dated record, failures included.

From 20 calls in my LinkedIn articles since January (ledger on request): 9 resolved, 2 hit (one weak), 1 partly, 6 missed; 9 open, 2 unverified. The falsifiers held; my 85 to 90% confidence did not, so every new call ships with a lower number, like the 1 in 3 above. Method: [seven calls, seven falsifiers](https://good.arcs.care/blog/nftt/seven-calls-seven-falsifiers). Same shape as Mogg, a dated YES or NO resolved by the world, but 20 calls in ten months, not 10 a day.
[MIT-licensed tools](https://good.arcs.care) I built for my own work, free to use.
[Trust](https://arcs.care/trust), [privacy](https://arcs.care/privacy) and [terms](https://arcs.care/terms), in plain words.

bites.text: Zach is a ball of livewire energy who gets projects done with great velocity, humor and craft. He's a great Swiss army knife to have in the team.
bites.name: Gareth Kay

lede: A natural skeptic who put the habit to work: I pressure-test fuzzy ideas until they earn a keep or a kill, and I stay calm when the ground turns hostile. Cat maxis beware, I got that dawg in me.

Two decades of 0→1 and go-to-market across ad tech, e-commerce, health tech, public safety and security, alternative asset management and nonprofits, most of them regulated. Clients from pre-seed startups to PE portfolio turnarounds and Fortune 500 brands; most recently the platform behind 10 regulated crypto products at Grayscale. Next: Principal, New Ventures. The ask: one conversation with whoever owns that hire.
ARCS, which I built, keeps the dated record of what I kept, what I killed, and whether I was right.

tabs.lede: Your open application asks what I would own that you don't staff today, and why you'd move faster with me. My answer: a hatch desk, sketched to build with you, in the open.

blocks.text: Most funds call it a deal desk. Mine would keep each memo, its kill criteria and the record of every call in one place.
Every pass would be logged with its reasons and a recheck date. The bet is that a recheck finds a pass worth reopening; the two-week test below says whether it does. The call stays yours.
It sits on top of your Idea Engine: the agents find and draft, the desk keeps the record. Nothing gets built twice.
